nary_nodes.label: Google withdraws Earth AI tool
evidence: Google has rolled back its new AI tool that allowed people to create fake images on top of its satellite imagery, following a BBC Verify report in which experts raised concerns about misuse and the potential to spread misinformation.

nary_nodes.label: Google announces AI image generator integration
evidence: Less than 48 hours after the tech giant announced the integration of its AI image generator Nano Banana 2 into Google Earth, it said it was pausing the feature "while we work on implementing stronger guardrails".

nary_nodes.label: Google states policy violations observed
evidence: In its statement on Friday, Google said it had seen "people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies".

nary_nodes.label: Google Earth trusted for reliable view
evidence: "We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world," it added.

nary_nodes.label: BBC Verify tests AI tool
evidence: A collapsed Eiffel Tower, a sinkhole swallowing the Great Pyramid of Giza and Russian tanks in Ukraine's capital were among the images BBC Verify was able to create when testing the feature, which initially launched on Thursday.

nary_nodes.label: Henk van Ess creates fake images
evidence: Before it was paused, AI and misinformation expert Henk van Ess highlighted the risks the feature posed, by creating fake images of a non-existent nuclear power plant in Iran, a refugee camp on the US-Mexico border and a fake hospital in Gaza with a bomb crater next to it.

nary_nodes.label: Google states AI content contains invisible watermarks
evidence: Google said AI content created by its tools contain invisible watermarks to indicate that they are fake or manipulated, adding that anyone who is "unsure about an image" can check it using the Gemini chatbot app or use the Lens feature in its search.

nary_nodes.label: BBC Verify tests watermark effectiveness
evidence: Generally, BBC Verify's tests found this is effective with images generated by the new feature. But we also found it was possible to circumnavigate these checks and trick Gemini into saying these fake Google Earth images are real.

nary_nodes.label: External AI detection tools fail to identify content
evidence: Tests using external AI detection tools also in some cases failed to identify the Google Earth AI-content.

nary_nodes.label: BBC Verify bypasses guidelines
evidence: however BBC Verify found that small changes to prompts could be used to bypass these guidelines.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool rejects "hang traitors" prompt
evidence: For example, a request to create a "raised platform to hang traitors" next to the UK parliament was rejected.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool accepts less specific prompt
evidence: But when a less specific prompt was used, it was accepted and the image was created.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool rejects "Trump" prompt
evidence: We also asked the tool to mow the word "Trump" into the White House lawn, but it said it could not "create that image" based on its guidelines.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool accepts "community garden" prompt
evidence: It did, however, allow a community garden to be generated in the same spot.

Experts told BBC Verify the tool could be used to spread misinformation with the appearance of Google's legitimacy - and highlighted the potential for bad actors to abuse it.
He said Google had allowed "invented" imagery to be "welded to genuine coordinates, drawn on genuine imagery".
"The forgery does not have to look convincing on its own. It inherits the credibility of the map it was born on," van Ess added.
AI-detection researcher Henry Ajder told BBC Verify the creation of fake imagery in conflict zones could prove particularly "destabilising" when events are fast-moving and information is scarce.
Google initially said that guidelines built into its AI model would prevent the creation of imagery depicting "harmful topics"
